Arpita Singh: in the solitude of her studio
 The artist, who passed away earlier today at the age of 89, was a strong feminist voice in Indian art and found freedom in her work till the very end
 Updated - November 10, 2026 01:26 pm IST 
 Rohit Chawla READ LATER 
 SEE ALL 
 Remove 
 Arpita Singh in her studio in her Nizamuddin East apartment
 | Photo Credit: Rohit Chawla
 Know the artist
 Arpita Singh’s richly detailed oils and watercolours centred women. Everyday women, affected by everyday problems, set against the backdrop of the social upheaval and humanitarian crises of her times. “When I work, I feel free,” she told writer and curator Kishore Singh in 2018, when he, along with photographer Rohit Chawla, met her in New Delhi for their book Portrait of an Artist . “My paintings involve procedure, and procedure keeps me occupied.” One of India’s most celebrated modernist painters, her art was influenced by her work with the government’s Cottage Industries Restoration Programme as a freshly minted graduate (Fine Arts from the Delhi Polytechnic), where she met traditional weavers and artisans. She later pioneered a distinct visual language that merged modernism with traditional Indian aesthetics. Over the years, her style shifted from black-and-white abstracts in the 70s to Bengali folk art, to the detailed oils she is known for in the 1990s. The Padma Bhushan awardee brought a strong feminist voice to Indian art. — Team Magazine
 An excerpt from ‘Portrait of an Artist’
 Photographs by Rohit Chawla; text by Kishore Singh 
 Arpita Singh paints in a park-facing, light-filled room that she has sectioned off with a row of book-filled shelves, separating it from the rest of the apartment’s living areas in Nizamuddin East. Not many know that she is a voracious reader — “everything from William Dalrymple to Namita Devidayal” — and isn’t easily scared by their voluminousness, just as large paintings don’t put her off, even though arthritis sometimes makes it difficult for her to squeeze the paint from paint tubes that have hardened. Sometimes, she’ll call her husband on his phone in his studio across the wall to ask him to help her. At other times, their driver will be summoned for help. “He scolds me that I haven’t yet finished a painting even though it’s been so many days.”
 Arpita Singh in her studio
 | Photo Credit: 
 Rohit Chawla
 The artist photographed with her husband, artist Paramjit Singh, last year
 | Photo Credit: 
 Rohit Chawla
 In this, her new studio in a new apartment in the same neighbourhood to which the artist couple shifted a year earlier, Arpita’s work has changed, taken up almost entirely by words. The figure has been obliterated, replaced by letters. When she couldn’t find her earlier sketches, she started making new drawings. These consisted almost completely of words, snatches of lines or phrases that she liked and wrote down in a diary: ‘if only you knew’; ‘road to nowhere’; ‘become something else’…
 Wish Dream 
 | Photo Credit: 
 Special arrangement
 A highly regarded artist, she combines the anxieties of a woman’s interior world with humankind’s existential threats, quite literally the guns and roses of everything from patriarchy to threats of terrorism and violence. Her drawings are dense, appearing like redacted sections of a proofreader’s text. The paintings, contrarily, are saturated with colour. Emotionally, though, they fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle in a nervous world continuously mired by fear of the other.
 Arpita Singh's Searching Sita Through Torn Papers, Paper Strips and Labels at the 2023 Kochi-Muziris Biennale
 | Photo Credit: 
 Getty Images
 For someone whose work reflects the apprehensive, Arpita feels freest in her studio, a place where she lets her guard down so her viewers can put theirs up. In this, the autumn of her career, she paints to keep darkness and loneliness in abeyance. “When I work, I feel free,” she says. “My paintings involve procedure, and procedure keeps me occupied.” The studio then, is her place of solace.
 Co-published by Kiran Nadar Museum of Art and Mapin Publishing 
 GALLERISTS ON ARPITA SINGH
 “She was a painter’s painter and inhabited a world of her own. It was the visualising in her practice that allowed us voyeurs to get a glimpse of this pictorial space that she spoke with.” Sharan Apparao Founder of Apparao Galleries 
 Sharan Apparao
 | Photo Credit: 
 Special arrangement
 Ayesha Kidwai; the painting is named after a neighbour who was a recurring ‘girl-woman’ face in Singh’s work
 | Photo Credit: 
 Special arrangement
 “I find it difficult to put into words what Arpita Singh meant to me. She was so much more than an artist I deeply admired. She was equally a friend and a constant source of wonder. She taught me not to overthink art or life, to find wit and wonder in the smallest things, to stay curious, and to always look at the world with a little more humour and imagination. I feel incredibly fortunate to have spent time with her, learnt from her and shared so many special moments with her. The world feels a little less magical without her in it.” Roshini Vadehra Founder, Vadehra Art Gallery 
 Roshini Vadhera
 | Photo Credit: 
 Gulshan Sachdeva
 Arpita Singh at work
 | Photo Credit: 
 Courtesy of Vadehra Art Gallery
 The writer is an artist whose lens has captured the pulse of contemporary India.
